### Reviewer 2

The manuscript by Khouri-Farah et al describes a novel dataset derived from single-nucleus RNA-seq analysis of human embryonic face and head development across weeks 4-8 after conception. They define several broad classes of cell types, including epithelial and mesenchymal, and a population defined as neural crest, and delve deeper into the cell identities by sub-clustering. Further, they perform a similar analysis using approximately equivalent stages of mouse embryogenesis and compare and contrast the data obtained between the two species. The authors next used a published human spatial transcriptomics dataset as a means to validate several of their findings concerning their human assignments. The human single-nucleus RNA-seq data are also used in conjunction with several public databases to make predictions concerning disease associations, human facial shape variation, connections between human and Neanderthal facial morphology, and clefting genetics. Overall, the dataset is a valuable additional resource for people interested in human embryonic head development that adds to other bulk, single-cell, and spatial datasets focused on the entire embryo. However, there are several significant issues with the manuscript, particularly with the analysis and interpretation of the datasets, that considerably reduce its impact and utility.

Major issues
1. The manuscript is too long, and there are many sections that are redundant or repetitive. The journal’s instructions for authors state that ideally the main text should be 5,000 words. This manuscript is well over 10,000 words, with the discussion alone about 3,000 words. Much of the data from the results section is reiterated in the discussion and there are paragraphs dealing with disease correlation analyses of red blood cells and immune cells that are not pertinent for an analysis focused on the craniofacial region. For example, the paragraph beginning on line 191 concerning ontologies associated with red blood cells including malaria or hemolytic anemia or the paragraph beginning on line 203 concerning immune cell related diseases. The length of the manuscript and its multiple individual correlations with other datasets means that the focus of the paper is lost, and the key points are difficult to extract from the study. Overall, the manuscript would be more impactful if it was considerably shortened and focused on key findings concerning the craniofacial region.
2. A major flaw in the manuscript is a lack of clarity concerning the regions under analysis in the sn-RNA-seq study. For human, only the following statements are provided: Results “we profiled the entire craniofacial prominence” and Methods “Primary human craniofacial tissues were obtained”. For mouse: Results “we generated single-nucleus gene expression from mouse craniofacial tissue. These samples reflected the major morphological landmarks of the human tissue profiled allowing a more direct comparison of cell types”. Methods “primary mouse craniofacial tissues … were pooled”. Unfortunately, these extremely limited descriptions do not provide sufficient information to understand or review the manuscript with any degree of certainty. One illustration of how this lack of detail affects the manuscript is that – as illustrated in Figure 6 - the craniofacial human ectoderm samples contain tissues related to the optic and otic placodes as well as to the neck (thyroid). These findings indicate a much greater region of the head and neck were surveyed than just the craniofacial prominences shown in Figure 1 and it is imperative to know the morphological boundaries that were used for the dissections.
As another example, on line 116, describing clusters expressing TUBB3 and MAP2: “We reasoned these clusters were derived from developing brain tissue not directly part of the craniofacial structures”. In removing these “brain clusters” their sample size decreased from 86,359 nuclei to 42,131, a drop of over half. These data indicate that their dissections of craniofacial tissue were not precise but included a majority of cells from other regions of the head. On the other hand, throwing away cells with expression of these two markers likely means they are losing cells from critical craniofacial structures, particularly the trigeminal ganglia. The authors indicate that the mouse data were obtained and processed in a similar manner, but it would be valuable to know if it required excluding Tubb3 and Map2 cells, and if so what percentage of mouse cells were removed from the analysis to help determine equivalence of dissections.
These considerations are especially important when the authors discuss the idea that there are multiple marker genes that were only expressed in a single species (Results: Section titled “Species-specific differences in marker gene expression during human and mouse craniofacial development”). Examination of the data provided in Table 20, for example, states that genes including ALX3, DLX2, DLX3, DLX5, and DLX6 are only detected as expressed in the human facial mesenchyme and not in the mouse “Only called in a single species”. This is certainly not supported by multiple other studies, raising concerns about the scope of the dissections, the data processing, and attention to detail in data analysis.
3. The question of anatomy and the regions dissected also has a direct bearing on the parts of the paper discussing the identification and analysis of clusters 1 and 6, called as mesenchyme and cranial neural crest cells, respectively. The mesenchyme of the head is derived from two major tissue-types, the mesoderm and the neural crest. Fate mapping studies have indicated that the majority of the mesenchyme in the craniofacial prominences is of neural crest origin, whereas mesodermal derived mesenchyme occupies areas of the head that are above and behind the developing eye. There is also a core of mesoderm tissue in the arches, including arch 1, that will form muscles of the head and neck. Therefore, it would be expected that a significant portion of the mesenchyme in cluster 1 would have a neural crest origin. However, the ratios of neural crest versus mesoderm derived mesenchyme will vary depending on the amount of tissue included from more posterior regions of the head. This consideration again makes it imperative to understand the boundaries of the dissections performed.
Even if a large amount of mesodermally-derived mesenchyme was present in cluster 1, there should still be a significant contribution of neural crest to this cluster. In this respect, when the authors subcluster the mesenchyme, they identify maxilla, mandibular and nasal prominence cells indicating the presence of neural crest derivatives. Therefore, cluster 6 should not be addressed as the only cranial neural crest cell population in their datasets. In fact, examination of cluster 6 suggests it may represent a few specialized neural crest derivatives – particularly Schwann cells as well as a few melanocytes. For example, as shown in Figure 3C, PLP1 - a prominent component of myelin - is expressed in all subclusters of cluster 6. Similarly, Mpz (myelin protein z) is broadly expressed in most subclusters. Together, these observations suggest that the mesenchyme has been mis-classified as not containing neural crest, while cluster 6 has been annotated as the major cranial neural crest population, whereas it represents highly specific populations of neural crest derivatives.
4. The authors define many subclusters in the mesenchyme, ectoderm, and neural crest but do not adequately describe how they were assigned to specific regions or structures. For example, for the ectoderm, TBX18 was assigned as a fusion zone marker, but it is not clear why, nor is it clear what fusion zone they are discussing anatomically. These issues of mapping and assignment are compounded by an absence of appropriate verification analyses. Here the authors rely on published data of spatial transcriptomics of two sagittal sections through a CS13 human embryo to overlay their expression data which are then presented in several figures throughout the manuscript. There are two problems with this approach. The first is that they are relying on just two sections and so it is not possible to determine the 3-dimensional expression patterns of any gene or cluster, meaning that considerable information is lost regarding assignment and anatomy. The second issue is that the resolution of spatial mapping was a 55µm spot, whereas an approximately 2µm spot would be required to accurately map a transcript to a single cell layer. Therefore, the study fails to link subcluster identity with specific anatomy at a meaningful resolution and in the absence of any other verification studies this significantly reduces the power of the dataset.

Minor issues
1. Line 462-463. “with LNP1 being more posterior and LNP1 being more anterior”. One of those should not be LNP1.
2. Line 625. “We found no enrichment in any cell types…”. This line is duplicated in the next sentence.
3. The authors refer to Li et al (reference 12) throughout the manuscript concerning mouse craniofacial data. However, this reference describes genome analysis of human brain data.
4. I have a number of suggestions for the images of the human sections. First, as the manuscript is focused on the head and face, it would be more useful to show only these structures rather than the whole embryo to reflect the focus of the paper. Second, orientation should be indicated on the panels: left/right (i.e. for Fig 4C), anterior/posterior, rostral/caudal. Third, it would be useful to have one or more annotated images describing the pertinent structures present in the images.
5. The figure legends for the Supplemental figures are missing. There was also no explanation of the information provided in the Supplemental tables.
6. Multiple instances: “this data” should be “these data”.

### Reviewer 3

The paper by Khouri-Farah et al., “Gene expression patterns of the developing human face at single cell resolution reveal cell type contributions to normal facial variation and disease risk” reports a single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) atlas of human craniofacial development from craniofacial tissues of 24 embryos that comprise six key time points spanning 4–8 post-conception weeks. The Authors describe seven major cell types, including muscle progenitors and cranial neural crest cells (CNCCs), as well as multiple subtypes of ectoderm and mesenchyme. Comparative analyses reveal substantial conservation of major cell types, alongside human biased differences in gene expression programs. The Authors also claim that CNCCs exhibit the lowest marker gene conservation, underscoring their evolutionary plasticity. Spatial transcriptomics is also employed to further localize cell populations, which should provide a detailed view of their anatomical context. Lastly, the Authors attempt to link these developmental processes to genetic variation, identifying cell type-specific enrichments for common variants associated with facial morphology and rare variants linked to orofacial clefts.

Undoubtedly, this atlas has the potential to offer critical insights into the cellular and genetic mechanisms shaping the human face, highlighting conserved and distinctly human aspects of craniofacial biology and linking them to the developmental origins of craniofacial disorders and the genetic basis of facial variation. This work could certainly provide an important resource for exploring craniofacial biology, with implications for developmental genetics, evolutionary biology, and congenital anomalies. Therefore, the study could be of interest and could fill a poorly explored aspect of human craniofacial biology by reporting studies conducted on human embryos as well as mouse embryos. However, there are multiple serious concerns regarding the current manuscript that need to be fully addressed. I list below some of the most salient issues that need to be resolved in order to increase the rigor and accuracy of the described findings, as well as supporting many of the conclusions.

Single-nucleus RNA Sequencing (snRNA-seq) Data Generation and Processing (Human Samples)
• It would be important to show a cartoon schematizing the regions of the human embryonic heads that were dissected. The Authors state that they processed the “developing craniofacial region” (quote) of human embryos from 4 to 8 weeks post conception. Lacking more detailed information, the reader is left guessing which parts of the developing craniofacial region were processed.
• How did the Authors generate the initial clustering of the major cell populations? Which Seurat version did they use? Which other packages were employed? All relevant information is lacking.
• More details are required in the Methods sections describing how the single-cell data were embedded and clustered, e.g. how many highly variable genes, PC dimensions, and nearest neighbors used to generate the UMAPS appearing in the main figures. Was any batch correction used? Were distinct embeddings calculated for the subset of neural crest clusters?
• It would also be important to provide separate clusters for each gestational time analyzed. This would highlight differences that are to be expected in cluster transcriptomes across the different gestational days, which are currently not clear.
• Why do the Authors use only TUBB3 and MAP2 as markers for neuronal cells that they want to remove from the query set? While primarily known as a neuronal marker, TUBB3 expression is also observed in non-neuronal cells and tissues, including endothelial cells, fibroblasts, spermatogenic cells, and stem cells, suggesting a broader role beyond just neurons. The choice of neural markers appears to be ill-informed and extremely reductive.
• Regrettably, there appears to be lack of rigor in tissue collection. It is of concern that the Authors lose half of their cells through the first filtering step. According to their statements, they started from 86,359 individual nuclei, but ended up with 42,131 remaining nuclei for their analyses. They concluded: “We reasoned these clusters were derived from developing brain tissue not directly part of the craniofacial structures. We therefore excluded these nuclei from downstream analyses resulting in a total of 42,131 remaining nuclei with an average of 4095 nuclei from each sample”. In summary, either the contamination of facial tissues by brain tissue was massive, or the Authors also removed cells that are not neural cells and thus could be integral part of head developing structures.
• The Authors state: “Early samples had consistently higher mitochondrial reads (Fig. S2d), potentially reflecting their higher dependence on mitochondrial output or an artifact related to lower cell numbers in the processing of each sample.”
This assertion is superficial and must be revisited. It is well known that high mitochondrial signatures are a strong indicator of apoptosis. The Authors have not unequivocally ruled out the presence of cell death in their samples.

Single-nucleus RNA Sequencing (snRNA-seq) Data Generation and Processing (Mouse Samples)
• Similar concerns are present regarding the isolation of mouse tissues. There is a lack of adequate information regarding the collection of the mouse tissues. Were mouse tissues also fresh frozen + thawed (like human tissues) or were they processed directly following tissue collection? Differences in tissue processing could heavily influence the snRNA-seq results obtained. There are serious concerns that the “species-specific” signatures the Author report might be due at least in part to differences in processing of the collected tissues, and they may not necessarily underpin species-specific identities.
The authors state that: “Samples were mechanically broken into single-cell suspensions” and that “Craniofacial prominences were collected in a very similar fashion to human samples”. What do the Authors mean by “similar”? Were neural tissue also removed in mouse craniofacial tissue dissections as it was done for human dissections? Or was there absence of neural contamination? All of these details, which have critical bearing on the reported findings of species-specific differences, are not provided.
• The Authors compare their datasets to those reported by the group of Trevor Williams (Li, H., Jones, K.L., Hooper, J.E. & Williams, T. The molecular anatomy of mammalian upper lip and primary palate fusion at single cell resolution. Development 146, 2019). But the latter datasets were generated only from murine midfaces and only at E11.5. This substantial difference in the datasets should at least be mentioned.

Neural Crest Cell Cluster (Cluster 6)
• What is cluster 6? It is not at all clear whether this is a biologically defined group of cells or a somewhat “mixed bag of cells” cluster. The Authors seem not to be completely sure themselves: “We then turned to the not yet concretely identified cluster 6 […]. We did not detect any significant pathway enrichments for this particular cluster (201). “The wide variety of biological functions and specific disease enrichments all suggested that this cluster might be enriched for neural crest cells. (208-210)”.
These descriptions are rather confusing.
• The Authors state that CNCC markers are significantly higher in cluster 6.
“When we examined a module of genes from regulatory networks recently identified in cultured human and chimpanzee cranial neural crest cells (CNCCs)69, we found significantly higher expression in cluster 6 (Fig. 2D).”
Which test or package or statistics did they use to reach this conclusion? Again, no relevant information is provided.
• Do all developmental stages contribute equally to the population in cluster 6? This information is lacking and is very important.
• The Authors state: “SOX9 and COL20A1 were more specifically expressed across the (CNCC) clusters, but again in non-overlapping patterns.” (261-262).
This sentence is very confusing. What do the Authors mean?
• There appears to be lack of a definite proof that Cluster 6 is truly a Neural Crest Cell cluster.

Spatial Transcriptomics
• There appears to be huge differences in between the two replicates shown for spatial transcriptomics (Fig. 3 E,F,G). For certain markers and modules the two replicates shown in the figure appear to be completely different from one another regarding the respective gene expression spatial features. Clearly
these human samples are precious and hard to collect, making it difficult to generate multiple biological replicates.. However, it is very hard to draw firm conclusions from these spatial validations.

Enrichment of Disease Genes and Variants Linked to Facial Variation
These analyses are hard to follow and very cryptic. Disease associations are correlative. Certain statements and conclusions do not appear to be based on rigorous supporting data. One example is provided below. The Authors state:
“Interestingly, while CNCCs certainly give rise to many of the downstream cell types and tissues, we found relatively few shape associations for CNCC subtypes” (531-532)
This statement is somewhat concerning, given that a rich body of literature directly links differences of facial shapes to variants in CNCC genes. The following review article comprehensively summarizes most of the relevant literature showing that variants in CNCC genes and enhancers underpin differences in face variation: Naqvi S, Hoskens H, Wilke F, Weinberg SM, Shaffer JR, Walsh S, Shriver MD, Wysocka J, Claes P. Decoding the Human Face: Progress and Challenges in Understanding the Genetics of Craniofacial Morphology. Annu Rev Genomics Hum Genet. 2022 Aug 31;23:383-412.
Interestingly, the Auhtors cite this review article in their “Introduction”.

Minor points
• Inconsistency in size of figure labelling (A,B,C etc.), legends in multiple figures (partially) overlap, image quality in multiple figures is poor.
• Lettering in some figures is exceedingly small and/or warped and thus very hard to read, even when zooming in onto the image or cartoon.
• The Authors need to revise the nomenclature for genes. Mouse genes should not be capitalized.
• Some of the references cited are not correct. For example, Ref 12 (line 146) is not correct.

Style and Grammar (only a few issues of many are reported below):
• 105: “after filtering for doubles and quality of per nucleus data“. Confusing sentence.
• 106/107: “Samples obtained from human embryos are more difficult to control what is collected”.
Sentence needs rewriting.
• 256: “TFAP2A was expression was observed in all clusters”. Sentence needs rewriting.
• 625-627: “We found no enrichment in any cell types for genes affected by de novo synonymous variants. We found no enrichment in any cell types for genes affected by de novo synonymous variants.”
The sentence is repeated twice.
• 758: space and period missing: “embryo25By“
• 815 f. Clip -> lip: “Failure of this region to fuse in humans has been suggested to cause cleft clip that could also involve the
nostril region and primary palate”
• 833: dominant or major: “Mesenchyme is by far the dominant major cell type”
• 993: describeD: “as describe for human”
• 1019: remove word duplication: “mouse genes were reduced and converted to those to those with one”
• 1058: space and period missing: “MAGMA89Frontal”
Lastly, this reviewer suggests careful editing of the text – in its present form, the manuscript appears to have been rushed and, regrettably, it is overall sloppy.

### Reviewer 4

The authors present a comprehensive single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) atlas of human craniofacial development, derived from 24 embryonic samples spanning six key time points during the embryonic period. Additionally, they integrate spatial transcriptomics data to further localize cell populations. Our findings shed light on the developmental origins of craniofacial disorders, the genetic basis of facial variation, and the evolutionary legacy of ancient hominins. Overall, this work provides a valuable new atlas for craniofacial biology, supported by comprehensive experiments.
However, there are still areas that require improvement. Specifically, some paragraphs should be refined or removed to enhance readability. At present, several sections in the Results are overly redundant, making it difficult to focus on the key findings. I encourage the authors to revise the “Results” section for improved clarity and readability.

My comments are as follows:
1. Beyond providing a more extensive atlas, have the authors identified any conclusions that Yankee, T.N. et al. (Ref 13) did not?
2. The authors state, “Closer inspection of the genes strongly expressed in these clusters revealed many canonical neuronal genes, such as TUBB3 and MAP2.” How did they quantify "strong" expression? Furthermore, they excluded nuclei derived from developing brain tissue. How can they ensure that all unrelated clusters from craniofacial structures were successfully removed?
3. Line 172: Why did the authors choose 100 marker genes per cluster? In contrast, in line 156, they selected only 10 marker genes to identify unknown clusters. What is the rationale behind these differing marker gene selection criteria?
4. Lines 172–216: The authors should refine these paragraphs to highlight the main findings rather than listing excessive details.
5. Line 973: It is unclear why the authors selected multiple resolution values ranging from 0 to 1 to identify clusters.
6. Line 1034: The authors should clarify how they preprocessed the spatial transcriptomics data quantitatively and in detail. Did they filter out low-quality spots?
7. Figures 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 share a common issue: they contain excessive information, making them overwhelming. The authors should consider moving less critical subfigures to the supplementary materials. The main figures should emphasize distinct and important messages for readers.

## Round 1 — Authors' Response

We thank the reviewers for their thoughtful commentary and feedback on our
manuscript and have diligently considered these suggestions to improve our work.
Specifically, we have considerably reduced the length of the text to refine the scope of
the manuscript, improve readability, and strengthen the rationale. We have also
included more detailed explanations of the anatomy and region dissected in both the
human and mouse samples that were used for snRNA-seq data collection. Furthermore,
we have reanalyzed the snRNA-seq data using previously presented as well as newly
suggested methods. To maximize the number of nuclei for downstream analysis, we
performed filtering on raw filtered barcodes from the single nucleus multiome
experiment, resulting in an increase of over 44,000 nuclei (130,427 in new analysis vs.
86,359 in previous analysis). We also removed neuronal and radial glia populations
using a new systematic method of generating module scores, resulting in the resolution
of roughly 54,000 additional nuclei (95,925 in new analysis vs. 42,131 in previous
analysis). When subclustering the putative CNCC’s, we labeled plausible SOX10+
Schwann using a similar module scoring methodology as described for neuronal and
radial glia cell types. We have also streamlined the comparisons with mouse
craniofacial samples and focused on conservation of cell subtype annotations on a large
atlas of mouse spatial transcriptomic data. Based on these new analyses, we have
updated all main and supplemental figures to reflect these changes in addition to
simplifying main figures to emphasize critical points and improve interpretability for the
reader. We believe these substantial additions have improved the manuscript and
addressed the reviewers’ concerns. We have also addressed each of the reviewers’
specific comments below (in blue). We also provide a version of the manuscript that
highlights all tracked changes in this revision compared to the original submission.
Lastly, we have substantially improved our online application that accompanies the
paper to include the new clustering as well as spatial transcriptomics data. We hope the
reviewers and editor find these revisions to be more than sufficient for publication.
